newsitem.title: USA: North Korea, KEDO site work to start soon - officials.
newsitem.headline: North Korea, KEDO site work to start soon - officials.

text.p: Work will begin within weeks to prepare the site in North Korea where the Pyongyang government and an international consortium will build two nuclear reactors, officials said on Wednesday.

The officials from communist North Korea and the Korean Peninsula Energy Development Organisation (KEDO), which includes the United States, Japan and South Korea, made the announcement in New York when they signed technical and policy agreements required to prepare the site.
The light-water reactor project has been negotiated by KEDO and North Korea over two years following a $4.5 billion deal signed in Geneva in 1994 between Washington and Pyongyang.
The isolationist Stalinist state agreed to freeze and ultimately dismantle its existing nuclear programme, which the West suspected was being used to develop nuclear weapons.

In return, Washington promised Pyongyang two light-water reactors generating 1,000 megawatts of power each by approximately 2003. North Korea was assured interim energy in the form of 500,000 metric tons of of heavy fuel per year for heating and electricity.

"This is the end of the formal negotiations on the issues that we have to resolve before we can begin work," KEDO executive director Stephen Bosworth told a news conference at KEDO headquarters in New York.
"I think that the difficult issues are really now behind us, now it's more a question of keeping the momentum of the project going forward."
Bosworth said the site preparation work would begin "within weeks" while North Korean ambassador-at-large Ho Jong said he expected the work to start in early August.
"I'd like to emphasise that we have laid another important milestone today in successfully implementing the agreed framework of 1994 and the supply agreement with KEDO in 1995," Ho said.

The complex technical and political negotiations over the past two years were suspended at least once when a North Korean submarine infiltrated South Korea in September 1996, raising tensions on the bitterly divided Korean peninsula.

"I'm confident that this work can begin within weeks," Bosworth said. "It is important to remember that we're not just talking about building a building, we're talking about creating a small town with all of the infrastructure that a small town requires."

Light water reactors such as those being prepared by KEDO and the Pyongyang government in Kumho in South Hamgyong Province have never been built in North Korea. They are less suitable for producing weapons-grade plutonium than the graphite-moderated reactors built by North Korea.

Bosworth said the consortium was still having difficulty raising the money to buy the heavy fuel oil promised the North Koreans, although he was confident KEDO's executive members would meet the commitment for 1997.

KEDO's executive members are the United States, Japan and South Korea, along with the European Union, which is in the process of formalising its membership. The general members are Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Indonesia, Finland, Argentina and Chile.
